overview: This card follows the Qatari polity from its late British-protected period through independence in 1971 and the continuing State of Qatar. The approximate 1938 atlas onset points toward the oil era, not national founding; the first oil strike actually came at the end of 1939. Six topology files generate seven displayed intervals, and world-1938.json contains the Qatar feature twice. Every imported outline includes the tested point at Doha but excludes tested points at Al Zubarah, Dukhan, Abu Samra and Al Ruwais, so the repeated peninsula shape is conspicuously too narrow in the west and clipped in the north. It is a classroom locator, not a legal boundary record.

periods.title: Oil search during British protection
periods.summary: The 1935 treaty renewal accompanied an oil concession; a 1939 strike was followed by a wartime pause as pearling declined.

periods.title: Oil exports and pre-independence institutions
periods.summary: Qatar exported its first crude shipment at the end of 1949 and built ministries and a cabinet before independence.

periods.title: Independent oil-producing state
periods.summary: Qatar declared independence on 3 September 1971 after termination of the British treaty relationship.

periods.title: North Field gas and a permanent constitution
periods.summary: North Field production began in 1991, while a drafted permanent Constitution was approved by referendum in 2003 and issued in 2004.

periods.title: Permanent constitutional framework
periods.summary: The 2004 Constitution organized the state; two-thirds of the Shura Council were elected once, in 2021, before the system was reconsidered.

periods.title: Amended Constitution and appointed Shura Council
periods.summary: Voters approved constitutional amendments in November 2024; Decree No. 42 of 2025 appointed 49 Shura Council members, whose first plenary session was held on 21 October 2025.

sections.title: Treaty, independence and changing constitutional rules

items.text: Qatar's 1916 treaty placed foreign and defence relations within a British-protected framework. A renewed agreement and oil concession followed in 1935. Oil was struck at the end of 1939, but the Second World War stopped exploration just as cultured pearls and global recession were already hurting the older diving economy. The atlas date of 1938 catches this economic hinge, not a birth certificate for Qatar.

Qatar declared independence on 3 September 1971 when its treaty relationship with Britain ended. The United States recognized it two days later and established diplomatic relations in 1972. Independence changed external sovereignty; it did not make the peninsula, its towns or its families suddenly appear. The official record is especially useful here because it separates declaration, recognition and diplomatic relations into three different events.

A draft permanent Constitution won 96.6 percent of votes cast in the April 2003 referendum and was issued in June 2004. In November 2024 another referendum approved amendments with 90.6 percent of valid votes. Official percentages report the announced results; they do not by themselves measure the openness of debate or how institutions operate after a legal change.

Thirty of the 45 Shura Council members were elected in 2021. Amendments approved in 2024 required at least 45 appointed members; Decree No. 42 of 2025 appointed 49, who held their first plenary session on 21 October. The Amir's 2024 speech argued that appointment better served unity and equal citizenship. That is the government's rationale, not an independent judgment about representation.

A short sample from current constitutional Article 1 is قطر دولة عربية ذات سيادة مستقلة, “Qatar is an independent sovereign Arab state.” Arabic is read right to left; an editorial transliteration is Qaṭar dawlah ʿarabiyyah dhāt siyādah mustaqillah. This is formal Modern Standard Arabic in a legal document, not a claim that every resident speaks the same dialect or uses Arabic in every setting.

sections.title: Pearls, hydrocarbons and the people behind the boom

items.text: Al Zubarah flourished for about fifty years in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries as a pearling and trading town linked to the Indian Ocean, Arabia and western Asia. Sand preserved streets, courtyard houses, fishermen's huts, walls and water works after abandonment. UNESCO inscribed the archaeological site in 2013. Its story is an antecedent to the modern state, and its pearl weights make trade visible without pretending diving was easy.

The first crude shipment left Dukhan through Mesaieed on 31 December 1949. North Field natural-gas production began in 1991, four decades after oil exports started. These projects supplied revenue and energy for rapid urban change. They were major engineering and organizational achievements, but they depended on international technology, capital and workers as well as resources beneath Qatari waters and land.

Hydrocarbon wealth remains both strength and constraint. In February 2026 IMF staff linked Qatar's outlook to expanding liquefied-natural-gas capacity and growing non-hydrocarbon activity, while also listing climate stress and possible future LNG oversupply among the risks. The same review urged a knowledge-based economy with stronger skills, private enterprise and trade. A giant gas field can finance choices; it cannot make diversification automatic.

Much of modern Qatar was built and serviced by migrant workers. An ILO review in 2022 recorded job-change reforms, online complaints and elected worker representatives in some companies. It also found continuing obstacles: employer retaliation, unpaid wages, slow recovery of money and incomplete protection for domestic workers. Skyscrapers and stadiums are achievements only when the people who build and clean them are kept in the story.

sections.title: Home, hospitality and learning to listen

items.text: A majlis is a sitting place where people receive guests, exchange news, settle problems, pay condolences and celebrate weddings. Carpets, wall cushions and hot drinks make the setting comfortable, but the social skill is listening. Children learn manners and oral traditions by accompanying older relatives. UNESCO also notes women's majlis, including academic and literary gatherings. This is a living shared practice, not a floor plan required in every home.

Arabic coffee turns hospitality into a tiny choreography. Beans may be roasted and ground for guests; elders and guests are served first, the server pours with the right hand, and a drinker shakes the little cup to say “enough.” Poetry and memories may accompany it. Useful child fact: before asking for a seventh refill, learn the cup wiggle. The custom is shared across several Arab countries, not uniquely Qatari.

Falconry grew from hunting into a social and recreational practice. Families, mentors and clubs teach how to handle, train and care for birds, while modern practitioners also work to protect falcons, prey and habitat. UNESCO's multinational listing includes Qatar and emphasizes trust between bird and handler. A falcon is not a feathery remote-controlled airplane; training begins with patient care and reading an animal's behaviour.

Family life in Qatar is diverse because residents come from many countries. The Education Ministry's published snapshot described more than 300 private schools alongside public schools, with different curricula serving many nationalities. That means classmates may bring different languages, foods and school traditions into the same small country. National culture matters, but no single majlis, meal or household arrangement represents everyone who lives there.

Qatar's Education Ministry oversees public and private schooling, sets standards and invests in teacher training. Its published snapshot paired large public enrolment with a similarly large private-school population and described higher-education institutions serving local and international students. This is an institutional achievement with an ongoing homework assignment: resources and impressive campuses still have to produce strong, inclusive learning for very different pupils.

Primary medical care developed alongside the oil-era population boom. A WHO-hosted account traces clinics to 1954 and, in its 2013 snapshot, describes centres providing general treatment, dentistry, pregnancy care, vaccination, pharmacy services, laboratory tests, health education, home visits and hospital referrals. Medicine was therefore organized as more than a hospital building: prevention, babies' care, teeth and medicines all met families closer to home.

UNICEF's comparable 2022 estimates put safely managed sanitation at 100 percent, safely managed drinking water at 97 percent and open defecation at zero. Translation for the toilet-curious: nearly everyone was counted as using a system that safely handles waste, which is much more informative than saying bathrooms exist. National percentages still cannot promise that every toilet, worker accommodation or pipe is equally reliable.

That water success has an environmental bill. Qatar's 2025 climate submission says extreme aridity, low rain and high evaporation make desalination vital, while hotter and saltier seas can raise treatment costs. Coastal plants face sea-level rise and storms, and more desalination can demand more energy and produce more emissions. In a desert, every dependable tap is an engineering triumph connected to climate, electricity and the sea.

ending.text: Qatar remains a continuing sovereign state; the atlas's open future interval is a data convention. Independence in 1971 ended the British treaty relationship. Decree No. 42 of 2025 appointed 49 Shura Council members, and the Council reported completing its first ordinary session on 6 July 2026. This establishes institutional status only through that dated check; families and communities have histories beyond constitutional dates.
